https://hungarytoday.hu/mol-takeover-tal.text: MOL Takeover Talks for Serbian Oil Company Reportedly Enter Final Stage The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has extended until September 30 the license allowing Serbia’s Naftna Industrija Srbije (NIS) to continue operating, Serbia’s Mining and Energy Ministry announced. The extension is significant for Hungary’s MOL, which is negotiating with NIS’s majority owner, Russia’s Gazprom Neft, over a potential acquisition of its stake in the Serbian oil company. “The extended license allows us to maintain supplies while continuing to work on a long-term solution for NIS. Our primary goal is to ensure sufficient fuel for the population and the economy and to ensure that Serbia’s energy security is not endangered for a single moment,” Energy Minister Dubravka Đedović Handanović said, as quoted by Világgazdaság . The Pančevo refinery, NIS’s main refining facility, plays a crucial role in supplying Serbia’s fuel market. The refinery increased crude processing to around 13,000 metric tons per day in August to meet higher demand, particularly for diesel during the harvest season. Low water levels on the Danube are also making fuel imports more difficult by limiting river transport capacity, increasing the importance of domestic refining capacity. The Serbian minister said negotiations between MOL and Gazprom Neft over the acquisition of the Russian company’s stake in NIS have entered their final stage. She said the latest extension of the operating license was an indication that progress had been made and that there was a willingness to provide additional time to complete the complex transaction. The extension gives the parties until September 30 to continue working on the ownership and sanctions issues surrounding NIS, while allowing the company’s Pančevo refinery to maintain fuel supplies to the Serbian market. The agreement allows for the continued development of NIS and the continued operation of the Pančevo oil refinery. https://www.dailycamera.com/2026/10/10/c.text: By Community Editorial Board | openforum@dailycamera.com | Daily Camera PUBLISHED: October 10, 2026 at 4:00 AM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Members of our Community Editorial Board, a group of community residents who are engaged with and passionate about local issues, respond to the following question: The U.S. Supreme Court opened its latest term by hearing arguments over whether Boulder can sue two oil and gas companies for their roles in climate change. Your take? The Marshall Fire was the most destructive in Colorado history, and drought conditions caused by climate change fueled the blaze, which destroyed over 6,000 acres and 1,000 homes. Six months prior to Dec. 30, 2021, unseasonably warm weather turned the Front Range into a tinderbox. Fossil fuels, a leading contributor to climate change, are largely to blame. The Suncor refinery in Commerce City, which emits more than 886,000 tons of heat-trapping greenhouse gas a year, is less than twenty miles from where the Marshall Fire started. Coloradans want to know if there is a cause-and-effect relationship. In April 2018, the Boulder County Commissioners sued the two oil companies for damages that resulted in drought, fire and floods. The damage has been done. Suncor and Exxon have “knowingly and substantially,” according to Boulder’s lawsuit, exacerbated the climate crisis through the sale of fossil fuels while they “concealed and misrepresented” the danger of their products. Reparations could cost the oil companies billions and open the floodgates for other municipalities to initiate litigation. So Goliath is taking David to the Supreme Court. Kannon K. Shanmagan, lead defense attorney for Suncor and Exxon, argued that it is an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” while Boulder claims such cases must be heard in state courts where the violations occurred. This is more than a simple matter of jurisdiction. Oil companies have exploited our national landscape for decades. Greenhouse gas emissions not only originate from inside Colorado but come from outside the state as well. How can one ascribe responsibility in such an interconnected environment? The devil is not only in the details but in the air we breathe, and that devil crosses borders constantly. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself. If the eight justices stalemate in a four-to-four tie, that would leave in place a Colorado Supreme Court ruling from May 2025, which would allow the lawsuit to proceed in state court. The oil companies do not want to go to state court, which is why they are asking the Supreme Court to intervene. Corey Riday-White, legal director for The Center for Climate Integrity, notes, “It’s clear the fossil fuel industry doesn’t want the damning evidence of their climate lies to be presented at trial.” Attorneys for the oil companies assert that since the Green New Deal has been foreclosed, this is a way for climate activists to advance their agenda through the courts, as they failed to do so through legislation. Exxon, whose total earnings in 2025 exceeded $28 billion, has continually lobbied the Trump administration for weaker environmental regulation and has donated $1 million to the Donald Trump Inauguration / Transfer Fund and another million to Trump’s Freedom 250. Exxon contributed nothing to the Marshall Fire Relief Fund. The current Trump administration is aligned with the fossil fuel industry’s interests. Neither the executive nor legislative branch will hold polluters accountable or protect the public from them. The judiciary must allow Boulder to have its day in court. State Court. Jim Vacca, jamespvacca1@gmail.com As the Beach Boys once said , “Wouldn’t it be nice…” If Suncor and other energy companies were held accountable for the death and destruction associated with their policies, decisions and actions that have ended up poisoning us and our planet. If the rapists, police, district attorneys and University administrators were held accountable for Jane Doe’s assault and the subsequent cover-up. If Jeffry Epstein and all his “associates” were held accountable for their crimes against girls and women. If Kristi Noem were held accountable for the unconstitutional tactics undertaken during her tenure (and, of course, for the dog). If Donald Trump were held accountable for his abuses of power, graft and other crimes. You get the idea. Examples of injustice seem to be everywhere. At the same time, accountability for these actions seems to be in extremely short supply: ICE has become less visible; energy companies are using legal gymnastics to obfuscate; district attorneys, police and university officials are playing public relations games with major crimes; Donald Trump has been granted immunity… As I began this editorial, the Beach Boys’ utopian wish came to mind, and I found myself wondering if it was time to add “accountability” to the endangered species list. And then my ballot arrived in the mail, and I remembered two other memorable quotes: “The vote is precious. It’s almost sacred. It is the most powerful nonviolent instrument or tool that we have in a democratic society, and we must use it,” John Lewis said. And: “Thank you for believing that it can be done. Thank you for believing that we can change our fate. Thank you for believing that we, ourselves, the Hungarian people, write our own history,” Péter Magyar said. Despite all the assaults on our form of government, our right to vote seems to have survived — at least for this election and at least for some of us. At the same time, the precarity of our democracy and the potential for intimidation and outright voter suppression on Nov. 3, Election Day, means that those of us who have retained the right to vote without risking arrest, detention or deportation have a responsibility to use our remaining leverage to save ourselves, our country and our de facto and de jure disenfranchised fellow citizens and immigrant neighbors. As the midterm elections approach, we must resist the impulse to simply give up in the face of these and other injustices. We must act in the short term while keeping our eyes on the long term. No matter how powerless and defeated we may feel, it is absolutely imperative to vote as if our individual behavior will make a difference; only then will our hope transform itself into a self-fulfilling prophecy. The midterm elections will not make all our wishes come true. But they may start the process of restoring the ideals that really do have a chance of “making America great.” On Nov. 4, the day after the election, wouldn’t it be nice to echo the words spoken by Péter Magyar and celebrate how we, like the Hungarians, believed we could change our fate and reclaimed our own narrative?
